STOLEN BATTERIES - Alternative energy fueled by crime

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We exposed a crime network targeting mobile networks feeding the alternative energy market created by loadshedding while every day South Africans foot the bill.

Unique Selling Point:
- a criminal element that indirectly effects every single South African
- Exclusive CCTV footage
- lekker undercover sting
- BUST

Summary:
Loadshedding is creating a market for thieves to target mobile network towers stealing deep cycle batteries. CCTV footage reveals the extent these criminal syndicates go to, to steal these batteries. We investigate the market helping stolen goods into the homes of unknowing South Africans.




Further information:
We all hate loadshedding. We are about to hate it even more. It’s costing you money indirectly. Thieves are stealing mobile network batteries and selling them as a solar solution for loadshedding to the domestic market. It costs the mobile networks roughly R200 million each every year in damaged infrastructure – repairs and replacement batteries. The reality is as long as the networks are losing that kind of money we as consumers are paying for it because they are still making profits, we pick up the tab in our fees.

WHERE DO THESE BATTERIES END UP
The biggest market for these batteries was our neighbouring countries – while they still head out the country – there is a growing market here in SA with loadshedding. Criminals used to sell the batteries predominantly on online platforms, but have branched out to physical shops. Small time suppliers are buying these batteries and offering solar deep cycle battery solutions for domestic use – these sell like hotcakes and often these suppliers have become the middlemen in a criminal network without realising the batteries are stolen. These stores are not spaza shops in informal settlements – these are stores in suburban neighbourhoods.

These batteries are used like a generator system in domestic homes – and are able to power a the basics in a household during power outages when installed correctly.

HOW BIG A DEAL IS IT?
EVERY SINGLE DAY MOBILE NETWORK TOWERS ARE TARGETED. EVERY SINGLE DAY. And it’s going to get worse with loadshedding, because there is a bigger demand for alternative energy solutions. There are multiple splinter syndicates operating around the country – currently Gauteng is the hardest hit because of the concentration of mobile towers in the region.

HOW THE BATTERIES WORK FOR THE NETWORKS
A mobile network tower can have up to 20 of these deep cycle batteries – the idea is when the power goes out – our networks stay up running on battery power. But when they’ve been knocked and the batteries stolen – when loadshedding kicks in, the network won’t come back on – leaving emergency services at risk and consumers disconnected from the world.

THE GRINDER GANGS
Teams of up to four criminals come armed with grinders and tools to break out deep cycle batteries in mobile network towers. They are so brazen they steal in broad day light. This isn’t easy work – it requires some skill and tools to get the batteries out and to get them away – we’re talking 60kg batteries.

* WE HAVE EXCLUSIVE CCTV FOOTAGE OF THESE GANGS IN ACTION, AND OF STINGS WHERE SOME INVESTIGATORS HAVE CHASED AND APPREHENDED THEM.

WHAT ARE THE COPS DOING
Not much as usual. While this type of crime fall as the Criminal Matters Amendment Act in terms of Essential Infrastructure related crime – these cases are not getting the same kind of attention as the non-ferrous metal cases because currently there is no dedicated police unit dealing with these matters.

It’s up to the networks to employ dedicated investigators to tackle this crime trend, to track and trace the criminals and to attempt to recover their stolen assets.

These teams use intelligence gathering methods, incorporating social media profiling and back tracing online ads to catch these criminals.

INTERVIEWS
- DEEP CYCLE BATTERY EXPERT – SOMEONE TO EXPLAIN HOW IT WORKS IN MOBILE TOWERS AND HOW IT’s USED AS A HOME SOLUTION
- INFORMANT
- SOMEONE TO EXPLAIN THE STING
- SOMEONE TO EXPLAIN THE BACKGROUND PROFILING
- BUST

Press Release:


Off-the-Grid with Stolen Mobile Mast Batteries
Are you planning to combat load-shedding with an off-the-grid solution of solar panels and deep-cycle batteries? Do you think you’ve spotted a bargain for this potentially pricey set-up? Beware of stepping into the clutches of a new criminal network as thieves target mobile network towers for their batteries. Carte Blanche takes to the air in a high-stakes chase with network providers to run down these brazen thieves as we investigate the crime that is getting stolen goods into the homes of unsuspecting consumers
Producer: Nicky Troll
Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender


Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: The effects of power cuts go beyond just being plunged into darkness, it can even cut you off from your mobile network when the power goes out.

While networks have back-up battery systems in place - there is a criminal element at work crippling communication networks.

LINK: These batteries have become a hot commodity with criminal syndicates targeting cellphone towers and stealing these deep cycle batteries for the black market.

ERNEST: This is national infrastructure we are talking about – it is damage to the economy, it’s damage to the country
VO: Ernest Paul is from MTN’s national network operations– he says the knock effects of these thefts are far reaching when the networks go down.

ERNEST: Small businesses, homes, security all sorts of things are impacted because there is a loss of communication

VO: The grinder gangs are so brazen – they steel in broad daylight. Watch as teams of upto four criminals come armed with grinders and tools to break out specialized batteries inside mobile network towers – the job requires minimal skill, and a lot of muscle – with batteries weighing upto 65 kg.

This insider works closely with these gangs – he says it’s a lucrative business that can earn the thieves at least R10 000 a week each.

DEVI: is this happening every day?
INSIDER: I can say each and every hour // Cellphone tower batteries nowadays is the high crime in South Africa

VO: While we were filming, a call came through about a theft in progress – we diverted our shoot and took the sky to follow up this lead in our ongoing investigation.

LINK: We’ve just received a tip off – a cellphone tower has been hit – ground teams are following the perpatrators, we’re following by air – hopefully we can find some batteries.

VO: We met Waal de Waal from Bidvest Protea Coin at the scene.

DEVI: What’s happening?
WAAL: we received info from informer – vehicle with batteries on its way on the highway – we intercepted the vehicle on the highway with ground forces, BUST INT2 M1 // we called the police to assist ,they followed them to this point – when they off loaded, they apprehended and arrested them

LINK: 5 people have been arrested, there is a haul of batteries that have been discovered at the back of this property – total value – just under a million rand.

VO: Earlier in the day, the suspects allegedly hit a tower in Midrand stealing 4 batteries. On searching the property, a further 65 batteries were recovered.

LEONIE: I don’t think anybody realises how big this problem really is – we are currently at war with the battery thieves.

VO: Leonie Verster heads up Bidvest Protea Coin’s task team for network operators. In the past, these batteries were destined for a cross-border trade, heading to countries like Zimbabwe and Malawi.

But in recent months - this crime trend has evolved with the country’s power crisis.

LEONIE: the guys have now identified it’s more lucrative to sell within SA borders, they don’t have the transport cost, they don’t have the risk of being caught on the road… // so now they’ve got the demand – they can steal and they sell immediately

LINK: These batteries aren’t traded in dark alleys – no, they are advertised all over social media and online sale platforms …. and let me tell you where they end up - … to power your home.

VO: We got in touch with a person from Montana, in Pretoria, who sells these batteries to the public. Johan Botha proudly gave us a run down of the batteries he had on offer at his home.

OPERATIVE: wat is leoch?
BOTHA: Leech! Dis jou beste battery vandag op die mark – daar is nie’n beter battery.
WAAL: is hulle nuut?
BOTHA: Nee, nuut is hulle R25k plus bleasting – dis tweedehands – maar huslle is twee or drie keer wat dit al gecharge is – hy kan, ek dink hy doen 6000 cycles.
WAAL: Het hy ‘n waarborg
BOTHA: Nee, ek kan hom nie waarborg mos nie, dis tweedehandse battery.

LINK: This is not stock – this is stolen property. Each one of these batteries would either been in a cellphone tower or on its way to be installed in a tower. This is worth about R375k – and being sold illegally for roughly R120k – truly competitive prices when your suppliers are thieves.

ETTIENE: // I cant compete with these solar companies selling these batteries for R8000 – because that is not reality.

VO: In reality, these batteries cost between R25 and R30 000 - Ettiene Visser’s company Averge Technologies imports Leoch Telecom Litihium batteries and has sole distribution agreements with the mobile networks.

ETTIENE: Averge has the exclusive rights to the Leoch batteries in SA or southern Africa – no one else should have these batteries in their homes, because we will not sell to the public, so if you see this battery, and it’s this particular battery, then you know that its stolen.

VO: It was time to pay Botha a visit.

DEVI: Devi Carte Blanche – so you’re selling stolen batteries
JOHAN: Do i?
DEVI: Johan do the maths, if you say it’s valued at R25000 – you’re selling it for R8000 – there is something wrong
JOHAN: it’s secondhand – I buy it from the guys as secondhand!
DEVI: I’m telling you it’s secondhand stolen – that’s what I’m telling you
JOHAN: // I’m not stealing it. You can’t tell me I knew that it’s been stolen – I’m not bloody frontseeing – I don’t know who the guy is.
JOHAN: // I’m buying it at Builders, yah, Builders in Attridgeville.
DEVI: you’re buying these batteries at Builder’s Warehouse in Attridgeville?
JOHAN: yah Builder’s Warehouse… in the parking… //
DEVI: Johan are you kidding me? //– do you not think something is wrong with that – you’re not going to a proper supplier – you’re making like a skelm deal there in the parking lot.
JOHAN: According to me I didn’t do anything wrong

VO: After we left, the police searched Botha’s property and recovered 39 batteries belonging to MTN and Vodacom – he was arrested and charged for being in possession of stolen property valued at around R700 000.

Botha who bought from online sale platforms, put us onto his supplier, Moses. Posing as an interested buyer, Moses met with our operative to make the sale – he brought along two batteries at R7000 each.

DEVI: //I can tell you right now both these batteries have been stolen from the cellphone tower
MOSES: Is it? //
DEVI: Do you understand that in the end you are in possession of stolen goods
MOSES: Is it?//…. Cut off the heads… it’s easy…

VO: Moses also offered up his suppliers, that apparently told him , it was old equipment that had been replaced with newer models.

MOSES: Me and that one from Montana – we are the tail – we are at the back of even if you take me as, the cases, the problem will keep on.

VO: Investigators will take up the trail of so-called suppliers from here. Moses and his accomplice were also arrested for possession of stolen property.

Meanwhile the insider explained that getting arrested is simply part of the job.

DEVI: They not scared of getting caught
INSIDER: they are not scared even if they are going to steal they are carrying money like R15 – R20 000 – sometimes if they find police, the bribe the police and then they go out same time. INT2 M10// Most of them have outstanding cases, they run away for the cases INT2 M10 beginning.

VO: The networks are frustrated, because even when arrests take place, the suspects are often released and re-arrested on new cases within weeks.

DEVI Taking seriously?
ERNEST: it’s an education process, for them a battery is perhaps a battery but I don’t think they understand the extent of what it is and that we are dealing with national infrastructure.

VO: Some syndicates have wised up, and have taken to burning the base tower station after stealing the batteries, in the hopes of destroying evidence.

And in the meantime, it costs the mobile network industry hundreds of millions of rands in security, to protect infrastructure by incorporating armoured structures, battery safes and cameras.

ERNEST: The reality is that this is a massive increase in our operational expenses and in the end the consumer may pay.

VO: So while the consumer picks up the tab for criminality, there are multiple splinter groups and middlemen profitting off the local black market – so much so, that thieves actually steal for specific orders according to the insder.

INSIDER: Sometimes they already have the orders, So maybe I need 70 batteries this month – so it means you go and steal it and after you steal it, you call him and then they come fetch it.

VO: Criminals even offer a delivery service.

LEONIE: normal strip mall – this is where they stopped, this where they offloaded – you’d collect your batteries here – visible to all.

VO: This is footage from a sting earlier this year – watch as they make a delivery in a swanky car and start offloading batteries - the solar shop owners cooperated with investigators and placed an order. The so-called suppliers were arrested at the scene.

UPSOUND: FROM CLIP

VO: This crime wave is unwittingly fuelled by South Africans desperate to get off the grid with solar panels and deep cycle battery solutions.

Anton Janse van Rensburg bought an alternative energy system valued at R150k from E-vest - a company specializing in solar packages. He thought he was getting a good deal when the sales rep offered him an upgrade on the battery.

ANTON: Instead of the 9.6 KW battery pack I can have 4.8Giga Watt Lithium Ion battery – and I said wow! That’s great!
DEVI: did he use the word Leoch?
Anton: No, no, he just said a battery.

VO: Anton’s installation went well, and when there were issues with the system – he was promised a replacement battery. But when it didn’t materialize he contacted Averge who’s sticker was still on the battery.

ANTON: he said listen – that battery is stolen that’s bad news for you – I said, what? He said, yes it’s stolen. //

VO: Shortly after the call, a technician sent by E-Vest came to replace Anton’s faulty battery – with another Leoch Telecom Lithium battery – it was confirmed to be an Averge battery.

It seems the company may have some explaining to do. Upon investigation, the E-Vest shop address lead us to Power-Africa – the two companies are affiliated. A sales consultant took us to the admin office where the staff got the company director, Melton van der Merwe, on the line for us.

DEVI: The leoch batteries you’re fitting into some people’s homes you know that they are stolen?
MELTON: No!
DEVI: where did you get them from?
MELTON: NO, I promise you.
DEVI: Who is your supplier?
MELTON: It’s a guy in Johannesburg – I’ll give you his details.
DEVI: yah, who? What’s the name of the company?
MELTON: Solar edge or something like that

VO: Melton insisted that he was supplying new batteries with zero charge cycles at installation.

DEVI: I’m telling you at Anton’s house it already read 78 cycles – so it was not brand new.
MELTON: yah, then that one wasn’t but like I said it was already wrapped in boxes so according my knowledge it is new. INT2 M27

VO: Leonie confirmed that some syndicates do pass the stolen batteries off as new and it is therefore possible that companies like Evest may not know that the products are stolen property.

LEONIE: These we’ve confiscated // they destroy the original box. INT2 M2 as they are you can see they’ve been repacked.

DEVI: can you give me an order form or an invoice that proves where you buy these batteries from?
MELTON: Yes, I will send it through to you. //
DEVI: I’ll tell you what because I’m sitting here at your head office, don’t send through to me I’m going to stand here and collect from you – because I know it’s here somewhere on a piece of paper.
MELTON: No, it’s here with me. //
DEVI: // take a picture and whatsapp up me – but do something – alright?
MELTON: ok, I’ll do that for you INT2 M32
DEVI: Thank you very much, much appreciated.

VO: But Melton didn’t send any proof of his Leoch Lithium battery orders – he only sent through contact details of his supplier - Ali from Solar Edge - who also denied any knowledge of the stolen property.

ALI: I was owning that company before.
PRODUCER: Do you supply Melton van der Merwe’s company with Leoch Lithium batteries
ALI: That was long time ago, last year.

VO: Melton replied to our written queries unequivocally denying any knowledge that the property was stolen. He went on to state that the Leoch battery:

“…represents a very small percentage of batteries purchased and sold by them [us]” – he added that they get them from their supplier as new batteries, in sealed boxes. He also says the Leoch batteries are found easily on the internet.

Melton further questioned the exclusive import agreements on the Leoch Batteries, claiming that he was advised by Leoch International in China that any person can purchase and import their products, including South Africans. But that’s not quite accurate, Averge Technologies has the sole import rights on Leoch Lithium Telecom Batteries like the ones sold to Anton. Leoch confirmed that they only shipped these batteries to Averge.

Melton however agreed to make things right with his customers.

MELTON: // we have to take all that we’ve sold and replace it with other batteries for the clients – I really didn’t know.

DEVI: if you have battery like this at home – what does that mean?
LEONIE: You know you’re in trouble Brand new, second hand it’s a no go. you’re in possession of stolen commodities – and subsequently you are going to be dealt with accordingly


 
PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO: With the country’s power problems – alternative energy solutions are all the rage – but beware criminals are on the prowl and they could be selling you stolen batteries from mobile network towers.

PROMO 2
VO: Home owners desperate to get off-the-grid create the market for criminals stealing mobile network towers batteries – we expose this crime trend in an in-depth Carte Blanche investigation.

PROMO 3
VO: While alternate energy solutions are in demand, are they all legitimate? We expose a criminal network stealing cellphone tower batteries that end up in your homes.

WAAL: we received info from informer – vehicle with batteries on its way on the highway – we intercepted the vehicle on the highway with ground forces, BUST INT2 M1 // we called the police to assist ,they followed them to this point – when they off loaded, they apprehended and arrested them LINK: 5 people have been arrested, there is a haul of batteries that have been discovered at the back of this property – total value – just under a million rand. VO: Earlier in the day, the suspects allegedly hit a tower in Midrand stealing 4 batteries. On searching the property, a further 65 batteries were recovered. LEONIE: I don’t think anybody realises how big this problem really is – we are currently at war with the battery thieves. VO: Leonie Verster heads up Bidvest Protea Coin’s task team for network operators. In the past, these batteries were destined for a cross-border trade, heading to countries like Zimbabwe and Malawi. But in recent months - this crime trend has evolved with the country’s power crisis. LEONIE: the guys have now identified it’s more lucrative to sell within SA borders, they don’t have the transport cost, they don’t have the risk of being caught on the road… // so now they’ve got the demand – they can steal and they sell immediately LINK: These batteries aren’t traded in dark alleys – no, they are advertised all over social media and online sale platforms …. and let me tell you where they end up - … to power your home. VO: We got in touch with a person from Montana, in Pretoria, who sells these batteries to the public. Johan Botha proudly gave us a run down of the batteries he had on offer at his home. OPERATIVE: wat is leoch? BOTHA: Leech! Dis jou beste battery vandag op die mark – daar is nie’n beter battery. WAAL: is hulle nuut? BOTHA: Nee, nuut is hulle R25k plus bleasting – dis tweedehands – maar huslle is twee or drie keer wat dit al gecharge is – hy kan, ek dink hy doen 6000 cycles. WAAL: Het hy ‘n waarborg BOTHA: Nee, ek kan hom nie waarborg mos nie, dis tweedehandse battery. LINK: This is not stock – this is stolen property. Each one of these batteries would either been in a cellphone tower or on its way to be installed in a tower. This is worth about R375k – and being sold illegally for roughly R120k – truly competitive prices when your suppliers are thieves. ETTIENE: // I cant compete with these solar companies selling these batteries for R8000 – because that is not reality. VO: In reality, these batteries cost between R25 and R30 000 - Ettiene Visser’s company Averge Technologies imports Leoch Telecom Litihium batteries and has sole distribution agreements with the mobile networks. ETTIENE: Averge has the exclusive rights to the Leoch batteries in SA or southern Africa – no one else should have these batteries in their homes, because we will not sell to the public, so if you see this battery, and it’s this particular battery, then you know that its stolen. VO: It was time to pay Botha a visit. DEVI: Devi Carte Blanche – so you’re selling stolen batteries JOHAN: Do i? DEVI: Johan do the maths, if you say it’s valued at R25000 – you’re selling it for R8000 – there is something wrong JOHAN: it’s secondhand – I buy it from the guys as secondhand! DEVI: I’m telling you it’s secondhand stolen – that’s what I’m telling you JOHAN: // I’m not stealing it. You can’t tell me I knew that it’s been stolen – I’m not bloody frontseeing – I don’t know who the guy is. JOHAN: // I’m buying it at Builders, yah, Builders in Attridgeville. DEVI: you’re buying these batteries at Builder’s Warehouse in Attridgeville? JOHAN: yah Builder’s Warehouse… in the parking… // DEVI: Johan are you kidding me? //– do you not think something is wrong with that – you’re not going to a proper supplier – you’re making like a skelm deal there in the parking lot. JOHAN: According to me I didn’t do anything wrong VO: After we left, the police searched Botha’s property and recovered 39 batteries belonging to MTN and Vodacom – he was arrested and charged for being in possession of stolen property valued at around R700 000. Botha who bought from online sale platforms, put us onto his supplier, Moses. Posing as an interested buyer, Moses met with our operative to make the sale – he brought along two batteries at R7000 each. DEVI: //I can tell you right now both these batteries have been stolen from the cellphone tower MOSES: Is it? // DEVI: Do you understand that in the end you are in possession of stolen goods MOSES: Is it?//…. Cut off the heads… it’s easy… VO: Moses also offered up his suppliers, that apparently told him , it was old equipment that had been replaced with newer models. MOSES: Me and that one from Montana – we are the tail – we are at the back of even if you take me as, the cases, the problem will keep on. VO: Investigators will take up the trail of so-called suppliers from here. Moses and his accomplice were also arrested for possession of stolen property. Meanwhile the insider explained that getting arrested is simply part of the job. DEVI: They not scared of getting caught INSIDER: they are not scared even if they are going to steal they are carrying money like R15 – R20 000 – sometimes if they find police, the bribe the police and then they go out same time. INT2 M10// Most of them have outstanding cases, they run away for the cases INT2 M10 beginning. VO: The networks are frustrated, because even when arrests take place, the suspects are often released and re-arrested on new cases within weeks. DEVI Taking seriously? ERNEST: it’s an education process, for them a battery is perhaps a battery but I don’t think they understand the extent of what it is and that we are dealing with national infrastructure. VO: Some syndicates have wised up, and have taken to burning the base tower station after stealing the batteries, in the hopes of destroying evidence. And in the meantime, it costs the mobile network industry hundreds of millions of rands in security, to protect infrastructure by incorporating armoured structures, battery safes and cameras. ERNEST: The reality is that this is a massive increase in our operational expenses and in the end the consumer may pay. VO: So while the consumer picks up the tab for criminality, there are multiple splinter groups and middlemen profitting off the local black market – so much so, that thieves actually steal for specific orders according to the insder. INSIDER: Sometimes they already have the orders, So maybe I need 70 batteries this month – so it means you go and steal it and after you steal it, you call him and then they come fetch it. VO: Criminals even offer a delivery service. LEONIE: normal strip mall – this is where they stopped, this where they offloaded – you’d collect your batteries here – visible to all. VO: This is footage from a sting earlier this year – watch as they make a delivery in a swanky car and start offloading batteries - the solar shop owners cooperated with investigators and placed an order. The so-called suppliers were arrested at the scene. UPSOUND: FROM CLIP VO: This crime wave is unwittingly fuelled by South Africans desperate to get off the grid with solar panels and deep cycle battery solutions. Anton Janse van Rensburg bought an alternative energy system valued at R150k from E-vest - a company specializing in solar packages. He thought he was getting a good deal when the sales rep offered him an upgrade on the battery. ANTON: Instead of the 9.6 KW battery pack I can have 4.8Giga Watt Lithium Ion battery – and I said wow! That’s great! DEVI: did he use the word Leoch? Anton: No, no, he just said a battery. VO: Anton’s installation went well, and when there were issues with the system – he was promised a replacement battery. But when it didn’t materialize he contacted Averge who’s sticker was still on the battery. ANTON: he said listen – that battery is stolen that’s bad news for you – I said, what? He said, yes it’s stolen. // VO: Shortly after the call, a technician sent by E-Vest came to replace Anton’s faulty battery – with another Leoch Telecom Lithium battery – it was confirmed to be an Averge battery. It seems the company may have some explaining to do. Upon investigation, the E-Vest shop address lead us to Power-Africa – the two companies are affiliated. A sales consultant took us to the admin office where the staff got the company director, Melton van der Merwe, on the line for us. DEVI: The leoch batteries you’re fitting into some people’s homes you know that they are stolen? MELTON: No! DEVI: where did you get them from? MELTON: NO, I promise you. DEVI: Who is your supplier? MELTON: It’s a guy in Johannesburg – I’ll give you his details. DEVI: yah, who? What’s the name of the company? MELTON: Solar edge or something like that VO: Melton insisted that he was supplying new batteries with zero charge cycles at installation. DEVI: I’m telling you at Anton’s house it already read 78 cycles – so it was not brand new. MELTON: yah, then that one wasn’t but like I said it was already wrapped in boxes so according my knowledge it is new. INT2 M27 VO: Leonie confirmed that some syndicates do pass the stolen batteries off as new and it is therefore possible that companies like Evest may not know that the products are stolen property. LEONIE: These we’ve confiscated // they destroy the original box. INT2 M2 as they are you can see they’ve been repacked. DEVI: can you give me an order form or an invoice that proves where you buy these batteries from? MELTON: Yes, I will send it through to you. // DEVI: I’ll tell you what because I’m sitting here at your head office, don’t send through to me I’m going to stand here and collect from you – because I know it’s here somewhere on a piece of paper. MELTON: No, it’s here with me. // DEVI: // take a picture and whatsapp up me – but do something – alright? MELTON: ok, I’ll do that for you INT2 M32 DEVI: Thank you very much, much appreciated. VO: But Melton didn’t send any proof of his Leoch Lithium battery orders – he only sent through contact details of his supplier - Ali from Solar Edge - who also denied any knowledge of the stolen property. ALI: I was owning that company before. PRODUCER: Do you supply Melton van der Merwe’s company with Leoch Lithium batteries ALI: That was long time ago, last year. VO: Melton replied to our written queries unequivocally denying any knowledge that the property was stolen. He went on to state that the Leoch battery: “…represents a very small percentage of batteries purchased and sold by them [us]” – he added that they get them from their supplier as new batteries, in sealed boxes. He also says the Leoch batteries are found easily on the internet. Melton further questioned the exclusive import agreements on the Leoch Batteries, claiming that he was advised by Leoch International in China that any person can purchase and import their products, including South Africans. But that’s not quite accurate, Averge Technologies has the sole import rights on Leoch Lithium Telecom Batteries like the ones sold to Anton. Leoch confirmed that they only shipped these batteries to Averge. Melton however agreed to make things right with his customers. MELTON: // we have to take all that we’ve sold and replace it with other batteries for the clients – I really didn’t know. DEVI: if you have battery like this at home – what does that mean? LEONIE: You know you’re in trouble Brand new, second hand it’s a no go. you’re in possession of stolen commodities – and subsequently you are going to be dealt with accordingly PROMOS PROMO 1 VO: With the country’s power problems – alternative energy solutions are all the rage – but beware criminals are on the prowl and they could be selling you stolen batteries from mobile network towers. PROMO 2 VO: Home owners desperate to get off-the-grid create the market for criminals stealing mobile network towers batteries – we expose this crime trend in an in-depth Carte Blanche investigation. PROMO 3 VO: While alternate energy solutions are in demand, are they all legitimate? We expose a criminal network stealing cellphone tower batteries that end up in your homes.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We exposed a crime network targeting mobile networks feeding the alternative energy market created by loadshedding while every day South Africans foot the bill.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: - a criminal element that indirectly effects every single South African - Exclusive CCTV footage - lekker undercover sting - BUST
metadata.Summary: Loadshedding is creating a market for thieves to target mobile network towers stealing deep cycle batteries. CCTV footage reveals the extent these criminal syndicates go to, to steal these batteries. We investigate the market helping stolen goods into the homes of unknowing South Africans.
metadata.Further information: We all hate loadshedding. We are about to hate it even more. It’s costing you money indirectly. Thieves are stealing mobile network batteries and selling them as a solar solution for loadshedding to the domestic market. It costs the mobile networks roughly R200 million each every year in damaged infrastructure – repairs and replacement batteries. The reality is as long as the networks are losing that kind of money we as consumers are paying for it because they are still making profits, we pick up the tab in our fees. WHERE DO THESE BATTERIES END UP The biggest market for these batteries was our neighbouring countries – while they still head out the country – there is a growing market here in SA with loadshedding. Criminals used to sell the batteries predominantly on online platforms, but have branched out to physical shops. Small time suppliers are buying these batteries and offering solar deep cycle battery solutions for domestic use – these sell like hotcakes and often these suppliers have become the middlemen in a criminal network without realising the batteries are stolen. These stores are not spaza shops in informal settlements – these are stores in suburban neighbourhoods. These batteries are used like a generator system in domestic homes – and are able to power a the basics in a household during power outages when installed correctly. HOW BIG A DEAL IS IT? EVERY SINGLE DAY MOBILE NETWORK TOWERS ARE TARGETED. EVERY SINGLE DAY. And it’s going to get worse with loadshedding, because there is a bigger demand for alternative energy solutions. There are multiple splinter syndicates operating around the country – currently Gauteng is the hardest hit because of the concentration of mobile towers in the region. HOW THE BATTERIES WORK FOR THE NETWORKS A mobile network tower can have up to 20 of these deep cycle batteries – the idea is when the power goes out – our networks stay up running on battery power. But when they’ve been knocked and the batteries stolen – when loadshedding kicks in, the network won’t come back on – leaving emergency services at risk and consumers disconnected from the world. THE GRINDER GANGS Teams of up to four criminals come armed with grinders and tools to break out deep cycle batteries in mobile network towers. They are so brazen they steal in broad day light. This isn’t easy work – it requires some skill and tools to get the batteries out and to get them away – we’re talking 60kg batteries. * WE HAVE EXCLUSIVE CCTV FOOTAGE OF THESE GANGS IN ACTION, AND OF STINGS WHERE SOME INVESTIGATORS HAVE CHASED AND APPREHENDED THEM. WHAT ARE THE COPS DOING Not much as usual. While this type of crime fall as the Criminal Matters Amendment Act in terms of Essential Infrastructure related crime – these cases are not getting the same kind of attention as the non-ferrous metal cases because currently there is no dedicated police unit dealing with these matters. It’s up to the networks to employ dedicated investigators to tackle this crime trend, to track and trace the criminals and to attempt to recover their stolen assets. These teams use intelligence gathering methods, incorporating social media profiling and back tracing online ads to catch these criminals.
